acceptance: Both `sync` calls in the TPC-H and TPC-DS data generators are bounded by a timeout and a stalled flush is handled without hanging or failing generation: the run continues, the skipped flush is logged, and a clear warning says timing measurements may include unflushed writes.
A regression test makes the flush command block (a stand-in that sleeps past the timeout) and shows data generation returns within the bound, and fails on the previous unbounded call.
A search of `benchbox/`, `tests/` and `scripts/` finds no other subprocess call of a global flush or process-enumeration command without a timeout, or lists each remaining one with a reason.

The investigation records, from system logs (`log show` for the window around 05:22 to 07:35 local on 2026-10-01) and process records, what was the first stuck process, whether a mount, backup or sync agent was involved, why the stuck `lsof` processes were re-parented to launchd, and what cleared the condition. If the cause cannot be established, the item says so and lists what was ruled out.

Decide whether a hung validation session should be detected: the shared test lock is held by a session that makes no progress, and other agents queue behind it. Either add detection (for example a lock holder whose log has not grown for a bounded time is reported with its pid and worktree, never killed) or record why not.

If the periodic `lsof` poller (`moshi-hook serve`, installed outside this repository) is confirmed to accumulate hung children, report that to its maintainer with the evidence and record the report here. Do not change that tool from this repository.
context: Evidence gathered during the incident, read-only: the first stuck `lsof` started 05:22:48 local and new ones were still being added at 07:22; the `sync` processes had pytest workers or earlier test runs as parents; free disk was 174 GiB and disk throughput was 20 to 40 MB/s while it was stalled, so the disk was neither full nor dead; a single-file `fsync` completed in under 10 ms during the stall; after it cleared, 0 processes remained in uninterruptible wait and a fresh `sync` completed in under a second. One stuck `lsof` had the agent session that was running the validation as its parent, so the agent tooling may have started a few of them. Earlier in the day, intermittent 3-second delays when spawning a freshly created script child with a new session, and intermittent `unexpected EOF` errors from `gh`, may or may not be related; that link is unproven and should be tested, not assumed. Nothing was killed or changed on the machine during the incident.
description:
On 2026-10-01 a development Mac entered a stretch in which global filesystem flushes did not complete, and local validation hung with it. A `make pr-preflight` run stopped making progress in its medium tier for over an hour: the pytest workers were asleep, several `sync` child processes were stuck under them in uninterruptible I/O wait, and the session held the shared test lock (`~/.benchbox/test.lock`), so other agents' runs queued behind it. Single-file `fsync` kept working throughout, so only global flushes and process enumeration were affected. It cleared about two hours after it began, with no reboot, and the cause of the clearing is not known.

What is established: product code runs the global `sync` command with no timeout at two sites, `benchbox/core/tpch/generator.py` (around line 782) and `benchbox/core/tpcds/generator/runner.py` (around line 196), both as `subprocess.run(["sync"], check=False, capture_output=True)`. A process in uninterruptible wait cannot be signalled, so those calls cannot be abandoned, and any test or benchmark run that reaches them hangs for as long as the filesystem is stalled. About 136 `lsof -nP -iTCP -sTCP:LISTEN +c0` processes were also stuck, started about once a minute from 05:22 local by a long-running `moshi-hook serve` process; they were a symptom and amplified the load (load average reached about 96 as the backlog cleared). The root cause of the stall is not established.

Two separate pieces of work: (1) the product hazard, which is in this repository and is fixable now; (2) the machine-level cause, which needs investigation and may be outside this repository.
